newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: IMF's Camdessus offers backing for S. Africa.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Camdessus offers backing for S. Africa.

text.p: IMF managing director Michel Camdessus on Friday encouraged South Africa to accelerate its macro-economic programme, which includes foreign exchange reform and offered to support foreign reserves.
Camdessus, on his first official visit to post-apartheid South Africa, assured a hostile committee of legislators that South Africa and not the International Monetary Fund would design any package.
Defending IMF interventions elsewhere in Africa, he said economic growth on the continent now averaged five percent, while South Africa could not hope for more than 3.5 percent growth this year.

"This would suggest that raising South Africa's growth rate at least to the level of other countries is feasible and worth pursuing," he added. The IMF, which so far has loaned the country $900 million to help pay the costs of the transition from white rule to democracy in 1994, would be willing "to support your exchange reserves and to provide you with financing if it appears to your government desirable."
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told reporters later there had been no discussion about a loan or terms for an IMF facility of any sort.
"There has been no agreement on any loan. No loan, no amount and therefore no conditionality," he said.

Responding to market rumours that Camdessus' sudden visit was linked to the negotiation of reserve support to enable the rapid dismantling of remaining foreign exchange controls, Manuel said: "The key question is why we would seek such a facility...I think we would take a fairly wide view, I don't think that we would say the objective is the liberalisation of the capital account and therefore we will utilise the standby facility only for that objective."
The abolition of remaining foreign exchange controls, which only affect residents and privatisation of state assets are the key conditions set by foreign businessmen for investment.
Camdessus also declined to deny the speculation outright, saying the world was waiting for the detailed implementation of the macro-economic framework published on June 14.
He listed revenue and expenditure details in the March budget, tariff policies, labour market flexibility, debt management and privatisation as issues that needed to be fleshed out.

"If then it were to be considered that it would be good to receive some support, some strengthening of exchange reserves -- for the IMF to extend a standby, for instance, in order to have the reserves built up, not so much with the purpose of spending them -- well, providing the specifications are well established, I believe the IMF wouldn't have major difficulty in supporting it," he said.
In an apparent reference to Camdessus' encounter with members of parliament, Manuel acknowledged "there has of course been some polemic."
But he said the debate was a healthy part of the democratic process and forecast it would continue as long as the country had a relationship with the IMF.
In views that Camdessus strongly rejected, members of the ruling African National Congress accused the IMF of causing more pain than progress in Africa.
